paras: The attempted lynching of John and Cicero Poe was a series of efforts in February 1881 by crowds at Winchester, Franklin County, Tennessee, to seize two brothers held on a charge of murdering a young man named Baker. Militia sent by the governor guarded the prisoners and on February 19 took them to Nashville past an armed crowd, and no one was killed. The episode ran in wire reports nationwide and set off an editorial dispute in Tennessee over mob rule in Franklin County.

According to the Pulaski Citizen, Baker was shot when he came upon robbers in a store at Owl Hollow; the Winchester Home Journal dated the killing to February 8. The brothers were arrested at the Swiss colony of Gruetli on February 13, identified by a clerk from the robbed store, and brought to Winchester jail on February 16.

A Winchester dispatch that day said there was "talk" of lynching but that the guard was too strong for an attempt. A Nashville wire said a crowd boarded a train at Tullahoma that night to go and lynch the Poes, but the conductor held the train. The Memphis Appeal reported that eighteen men demanded the prisoners at the jail on the morning of February 17 and left when refused, while the Pulaski Citizen placed "a small mob" at the jail that night. Judge J. J. Williams then telegraphed Governor Alvin Hawkins that the Poes would be lynched if the charge was proven, and the governor sent forty men of the Porter Rifles and Rock City Guards.

The troops arrived on February 18 to a crowd that shouted "We don't want you," put at under 500 by the Home Journal and at fifteen hundred to two thousand by the Pulaski Citizen. Early on February 19 the defense waived examination and the prisoners were committed to the Davidson County jail. According to the Chicago Tribune, two or three hundred armed people followed the troops to the depot shouting "Go ahead and kill them" and urging Baker's father to lead a rush. The father protested at the depot but declared himself satisfied after he was invited to accompany the prisoners. A broken bridge forced a march to Decherd, about fifty people following, and the Poes reached the Nashville jail that day.

From jail the brothers wrote that they feared being lynched if returned to Winchester without a guard. In April 1881 a Winchester jury convicted both of first-degree murder and they were sentenced to hang, then taken back to Nashville for fear of lynching or rescue. The Tennessee Supreme Court granted a new trial in March 1882, and no arrest of anyone in the crowds is reported.

The Nashville wire ran on February 18 in the New-York Tribune, the Savannah Morning News, the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer and other papers under heads such as "Attempt at Lynch Law." The Chicago Tribune headlined "The People of Winchester, Tenn., Attempt Another Lynching" and the Dallas Daily Herald "The Spirit of Judge Lynch in Tennessee," while the New-York Tribune called the brothers desperadoes "of the worst class." The Weekly Floridian cited the case as proof that the lynching of prisoners in Tennessee "still goes on."

The Pulaski Citizen's "A Mob Foiled" praised the troops, and the Nashville American, as quoted in Winchester, said they had averted "another of those terrible affairs." The Winchester Home Journal answered that "there were no mob men here" and warned that slow courts would "have to give way to the makers of the law—the People."

Accounts differ on whether the attempt was a train party, a morning demand or a night demand at the jail. The second brother appears as Tish, Lish, Fish, Tede and Thomas before the trial reports name him Cicero. The brothers' race is uncertain: the Memphis Appeal printed the judge's telegram as calling them "the two negroes," but the Home Journal's dated text of it reads "Two men by the name of Poe," and no other report gives a race. A wire digest in the Iola Register wrongly listed the Poes among men lynched at Springfield in another case.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of John and Cicero Poe
bases: Crowds sought to take two jailed prisoners and lynch them, by train from Tullahoma, by a demand at the jail and by an armed crowd following the troops; no one was killed (A2, A4, A11, A16).

Groups of eighteen to several hundred men sought to lynch the Poes over the Baker murder charge, but the guard and the Nashville troops kept them and both brothers were later tried, so no one was killed (A4, A11, A24); this is an attempted lynching.

The wire, the Memphis Appeal, the Chicago Tribune, the Winchester Home Journal and the Pulaski Citizen independently report crowds seeking to lynch the Poes and troops removing them to Nashville, though they differ on details (A2, A4, A11, A13, A16).

accounts.label: Pulaski Citizen

accounts.label: Chicago Tribune Nashville special

accounts.label: Winchester Home Journal
accounts.gist: The crowd did not threaten the troops and 'there were no mob men here'; the people wanted only a speedy trial.

accounts.label: The Poes' letter
accounts.gist: The brothers denied the charges and said they feared being lynched if returned to Winchester without a guard.

framing.detail: National papers ran the Nashville wire under heads such as 'Attempt at Lynch Law' and 'About to be Lynched'.
The Chicago Tribune headed its account 'The People of Winchester, Tenn., Attempt Another Lynching' and 'Saved by the Military'.
The Weekly Floridian wrote that the lynching of prisoners in officers' custody in Tennessee 'still goes on'.
The Pulaski Citizen's 'A Mob Foiled' praised the troops while calling the prisoners 'the Owl Hollow Murderers'.
The Winchester Home Journal denied any mob, likened John Poe to a 'mad dog or wild beast', and warned the law would give way to 'the People' if courts were slow.
